title: Character antiequivalence and scalar extension for groups of multiplicative type
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Group schemes are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and closed subgroups mean [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Write $\mathbf G_m$ for [def-sc-gm-ga]. A group scheme is of multiplicative type if its extension to an algebraic closure of $k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure] is a closed subgroup of $\mathbf G_m^n$ for some $n\geq0$. Fix a separable closure $k^s$ of $k$ [def-pd-separable-closure] and put $\Gamma_k=\operatorname{Gal}(k^s/k)$, with open subgroups given by fixing finite separable intermediate extensions. For an additive abelian group $M$, the group algebra $k[M]$ has basis $e_m$ ($m\in M$), multiplication $e_me_n=e_{m+n}$, and Hopf operations $\Delta(e_m)=e_m\otimes e_m$, $\epsilon(e_m)=1$, $S(e_m)=e_{-m}$. Set $D_k(M)=\operatorname{Spec}k[M]$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] with these group operations when $M$ has trivial Galois action.

Every group $G$ of multiplicative type becomes isomorphic to $D_L(M)$ over some finite separable extension $L/k$ inside $k^s$, for a finitely generated abelian group $M$. More precisely, the character functor
$$X^*(G)=\operatorname{Hom}_{k^s\text{-grp}}(G_{k^s},\mathbf G_{m,k^s})$$
(with pointwise multiplication written additively and Galois action by conjugation) is a contravariant equivalence from groups of multiplicative type to finitely generated abelian groups with continuous $\Gamma_k$-action for the discrete topology. For such a module $M$, choose a finite Galois extension $L/k$ through which the action factors. A quasi-inverse is the group scheme $D_k(M)=\operatorname{Spec}(L[M]^{\operatorname{Gal}(L/k)})$, with semilinear action $\sigma(ae_m)=\sigma(a)e_{\sigma m}$ and descended Hopf operations; its isomorphism class and its character identification are independent of $L$. There are natural identifications $G\simeq D_k(X^*(G))$ and $X^*(D_k(M))\simeq M$. Under this equivalence a homomorphism $f:G\to H$ is a closed immersion if and only if $f^*:X^*(H)\to X^*(G)$ is surjective.

For every field extension $K/k$ [def-pc-field-extension] and compatible choices of separable closures, extending characters gives a natural isomorphism $X^*(G_K)\simeq X^*(G)$ of underlying abelian groups, where the Galois action on the right is restricted along $\Gamma_K\to\Gamma_k$. These identifications are compatible with homomorphisms of groups and their character maps. In the split case they identify $(D_k(M))_K$ with $D_K(M)$.

source.place: Sections 12(a)--(c), especially Theorems 12.8 and 12.9(a),(b), printed pp.230--234; Corollary 12.19, p.238; Section 12(g), Theorem 12.23 and its Galois-descent construction, pp.239--240; split scalar extension in the proof of Corollary 12.25, p.240.

proof.text: Put $A=k[G]$. The coordinate Hopf identities in [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] translate the group laws. By the affine-spectrum Hom bijection, a character $G\to\mathbf G_m$ is precisely a Hopf map $k[t,t^{-1}]\to A$: it is determined by $a=t\mapsto a$, with $\epsilon(a)=1$, $\Delta(a)=a\otimes a$. The inverse relation imposes no extra condition since the antipode identity gives $S(a)a=aS(a)=1$. Conversely these equations make the algebra map $t\mapsto a$, $t^{-1}\mapsto S(a)$ commute with the Hopf operations, hence its spectrum is a group homomorphism. Products of characters correspond to products of these elements. This also explains the same dictionary over every field extension.

source.place: Sections 12(a)–(b), pp.230–232: characters as group-like elements; affine dictionary in Sections 3(a)–(b).

proof.text: Over $\bar k$, the defining closed embedding of $G_{\bar k}$ into a split torus and [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] give $A_{\bar k}\simeq\bar k[N]$. Thus its coalgebra has a group-like basis. Apply [lem-sfb-geometrically-diagonal-coalgebra-separable-basis] to $A$: all group-like elements form a basis of $A_{k^s}$. They form an abelian group $M$ under multiplication, inverse given by the antipode. The basis map $k^s[M]\to A_{k^s}$ is an algebra and Hopf isomorphism, since every operation agrees on each basis element. To see $M$ is finitely generated, take finite algebra generators of $A_{k^s}$, expand them in this basis, and let $M_0$ be the subgroup generated by their finite supports. The subalgebra $k^s[M_0]$ contains all the generators, so equals $k^s[M]$; basis independence gives $M_0=M$. Finally choose group generators $m_i$ and their inverses. Each corresponding element of $A_{k^s}$ has finitely many coefficients in $k^s$ relative to a $k$-basis of $A$. Adjoin these coefficients and those expressing finite algebra generators of $A$ as polynomials in these elements. They lie in a finite separable $L/k$. The group-like equations already hold over $L$ by coefficient injectivity, and the resulting $L[M]\to A_L$ is surjective by the chosen expressions and injective by extension to $k^s$. Hence $G_L\simeq D_L(M)$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-set-in-finite-galois-subextension] to the finite coefficients in the Galois extension $k^s/k$ to take $L$ finite Galois from the outset.

source.place: Theorems 12.8 and 12.18(d), Corollary 12.19, pp.233,237–238; finite coefficient argument for the last sentence of Corollary 12.19.

proof.text: For any field $F$, [lem-sfb-group-algebra-group-like-basis] says that the group-like elements of $F[M]$ are exactly $e_m$. Consequently a Hopf map $F[N]\to F[M]$ is uniquely $e_n\mapsto e_{u(n)}$ for a group homomorphism $u:N\to M$: multiplication forces additivity, and each additive $u$ defines a Hopf map by the displayed basis formula. Step 1 translates this into $\operatorname{Hom}(D_F(M),D_F(N))=\operatorname{Hom}(N,M)$, including $X(D_F(M))=M$ by $m\leftrightarrow(t\mapsto e_m)$. The evaluation map $F[X(D_F(M))]\to F[M]$ is the identity on its indexed basis. These formulas respect identities and composition.

source.place: Lemma 12.4 and Theorem 12.9(a), pp.232–233; basis calculation replacing the cyclic-case verification.

proof.text: The canonical semilinear action on $A_{k^s}$ permutes its group-like basis. A finite Galois splitting field from step 2 fixes that basis pointwise, so this is a continuous action on $M=X^*(G)$. Conversely, let $M$ be finitely generated with continuous $\Gamma_k$-action. For finitely many generators choose finite separable fields whose fixing subgroups fix each generator. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-set-in-finite-galois-subextension], their finite generating coefficients lie in a finite Galois $L/k$ whose fixing subgroup fixes every generator and hence all of $M$. The formula $\sigma(ae_m)=\sigma(a)e_{\sigma m}$ gives an action on $L[M]$ respecting multiplication, comultiplication, counit and antipode by direct evaluation on $ae_m$. Apply [lem-sfb-galois-hopf-algebra-descent]: $B=L[M]^{\operatorname{Gal}(L/k)}$ is a Hopf $k$-algebra, $L\otimes_k B\simeq L[M]$, and $B$ is finitely generated. Thus $D_k(M)=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is of finite type and is geometrically of multiplicative type: if $m_1,\ldots,m_r$ generate $M$, the surjective Hopf map $\bar k[\mathbf Z^r]\to\bar k[M]$ gives a closed embedding into $\mathbf G_m^r$ by [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Step 3 identifies its characters with $M$, equivariantly by the semilinear formula.

source.place: Section 12(g), pp.239–240, construction preceding Theorem 12.23; Appendix A.64, pp.580–581.

proof.text: For two multiplicative-type groups choose a common finite Galois splitting field $L$. Under the basis description, an equivariant homomorphism of their character groups gives by step 3 an $L$-Hopf map; equivariance on each $e_m$ is exactly commutation with the semilinear action. Full faithfulness in [lem-sfb-galois-hopf-algebra-descent] descends it uniquely to $k$. Conversely every $k$-homomorphism yields this equivariance, proving full faithfulness of $X^*$. For $G$, evaluation $e_\chi\mapsto\chi^*(t)$ is an equivariant Hopf isomorphism after splitting, and descends to $G\simeq D_k(X^*(G))$. The other composite is the identification $m\leftrightarrow e_m$ in step 3. Naturality follows from $e_m\mapsto e_{u(m)}$. If two fields are chosen in step 4, pass to their finite Galois compositum. Their scalar-extended Hopf algebras are the same indexed group algebra with the same semilinear action; descent gives a unique isomorphism inducing its identity. It preserves the character labels, and uniqueness proves compatibility for three choices. This proves independence and the asserted natural quasi-inverse identifications.

source.place: Theorem 12.23 and its proof, p.240; Appendix A.64 and A.66, pp.580–581.

proof.text: A map between affine schemes is a closed immersion exactly when its coordinate map is surjective, by [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Surjectivity of a $k$-linear map is detected after any field extension: choose a vector-space complement of its image; tensoring bases shows that its scalar extension is surjective exactly when that complement is zero. Over $k^s$, the coordinate map of $f:G\to H$ is $k^s[X^*(H)]\to k^s[X^*(G)]$, $e_n\mapsto e_{f^*(n)}$. Its image is precisely the span of basis elements indexed by $\operatorname{im}f^*$, so it is surjective exactly when $f^*$ is. This proves both directions without any smoothness or reducedness hypothesis.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(b)–(c), pp.233–234, and Theorem 12.23, p.240; surjectivity checked on the group-algebra basis.

proof.text: Let $K/k$ be arbitrary and choose $k^s\hookrightarrow K^s$ as in the statement. For every abelian $M$ the basis formula $\lambda\otimes e_m\mapsto\lambda e_m$ is an isomorphism $K\otimes_k k[M]\simeq K[M]$ of Hopf algebras: its inverse sends $\lambda e_m$ to $\lambda\otimes e_m$, and all operations agree on these symbols. Apply the same formula from $k^s$ to $K^s$ to the split description of $G_{k^s}$ in step 2. By [lem-sfb-group-algebra-group-like-basis], extending a character keeps its label $m$ and every character over $K^s$ has such a label, so extension is a bijection on characters and respects their addition. For $\tau\in\Gamma_K$, the conjugation formula on coefficients is the one for its restriction $\tau|_{k^s}\in\Gamma_k$, giving exactly the claimed restricted action. For $f:G\to H$, both orders of extending and pulling back send $e_n$ to $e_{f^*(n)}$; hence the character identifications are natural in $G$ and compatible with character maps. The same scalar formula proves the split-case group-scheme identification.

source.place: Theorem 12.23, p.240; split scalar-extension calculation in the proof of Corollary 12.25, p.240, extended by the indexed-basis formulas.

proof_origin.place: Theorems 12.8, 12.9(a), 12.18(d), 12.23; Corollary 12.19; Appendix A.64–A.66; pp.232–240,580–581. Basis and coefficient verifications made explicit.
